video_title: AI Agents Are Already Changing the Price of Goods | Odd Lots
gist: Lindsay Owens of Groundwork Collaborative lays out evidence that Instacart, StubHub, Uber and others use personalized pricing experiments, and discusses how AI shopping agents like Muse may help or be turned against consumers, with calls for fiduciary duties on agents and concern over algorithmic price coordination.

insights.claim: Groundwork Collaborative, Consumer Reports and More Perfect Union recruited 400 secret shoppers who bought the same 23 grocery items for pickup from the same store at the same time via Instacart, and 75% of items were priced differently across shoppers, with gaps up to 23%.
insights.speaker: Lindsay Owens
insights.so_what: Same-time, same-store price divergence shows randomized or personalized price tests are live in grocery e-commerce.

insights.claim: Groundwork estimated the Instacart price dispersion could cost a family of four as much as $1,200 more per year, using Instacart's own estimate of household spend.
insights.speaker: Lindsay Owens
insights.so_what: Gives a headline consumer-cost figure that drives regulatory and political attention.

insights.claim: Instacart bought Eversight in 2022, an AI platform for turnkey retailer pricing experiments run without consumers' knowledge; Owens says this is how her team knew to run the experiment, though Instacart maintains the price differences were randomly assigned A/B tests.
insights.speaker: Lindsay Owens
insights.so_what: Acquisitions of pricing-experiment tooling are a leading indicator of platforms industrializing price testing.

insights.claim: In a Today show test, 12 production assistants buying the same Harry Styles Madison Square Garden ticket saw constant ticket prices but StubHub fees varying by up to $60, dropping to about $4 in incognito mode; StubHub called it A/B testing, not personalization.
insights.speaker: Lindsay Owens
insights.so_what: Fees, not headline price, are where personalization hides, and browsing state changes outcomes.

insights.claim: A DoorDash patent described a 16-factor agitation index including battery life, scroll speed and scroll jerkiness, tied to promotions and menu ordering; DoorDash withdrew the patent after Groundwork exposed it.
insights.speaker: Lindsay Owens
insights.so_what: Shows the behavioral signals platforms consider usable for willingness-to-pay inference.

insights.claim: Uber has shifted from surge pricing to apparently maximizing what each rider will pay and minimizing what each driver will accept, as experiments with identical pickups and destinations produced varying rider prices and varying driver offers.
insights.speaker: Lindsay Owens
insights.so_what: Two-sided individualized pricing erodes the supply-signal justification for surge.

insights.claim: Willingness to pay is not the same as ability to pay, so surveillance pricing is unlikely to act as a Robin Hood cross-subsidy; firms will take the most from the rich, as much as possible from everyone else, and exploit urgent need such as a sick child.
insights.speaker: Lindsay Owens
insights.so_what: Rebuts the argument that personalized pricing helps poorer buyers.
insights.quote: I think where I am not so convinced is that that will be used as a cross-subsidy for everyone else.

insights.claim: Geolocation and IP proxies allow discrimination by protected characteristics without stating it; Owens cites a ProPublica finding that Princeton Review charged more in heavily Asian-American neighborhoods and knows of no federal body examining this now.
insights.speaker: Lindsay Owens
insights.so_what: Disparate-impact legal exposure is an unpriced risk for algorithmic pricers.

themes.theme: Profit models and the end of the fixed price

insights.claim: Pricing has shifted from cost-plus-margin stickers to engineered science, with companies hiring physicists and buying AI firms to run experiments to find the optimal price per shopper.
insights.speaker: Lindsay Owens
insights.so_what: Pricing power increasingly depends on data and experimentation capacity rather than cost structure.

insights.claim: Fixed public price tags date only to John Wanamaker's 1870s Philadelphia store, inspired by Quaker opposition to haggling; Owens argues they provide predictability and transparency that keep prices competitive, and that budget shoppers protect prices for everyone if they cannot be identified and picked off.
insights.speaker: Lindsay Owens
insights.so_what: Framing the posted price as a public good supports the case for regulation.

insights.claim: Airlines, after deregulation, pioneered yield management; dynamic pricing was rare outside them until Uber's surge pricing and Ticketmaster dynamic pricing in 2011.
insights.speaker: Lindsay Owens
insights.so_what: Dynamic pricing diffusion is roughly a 15-year story now accelerating with AI.

insights.claim: Companies are moving into new profit models: about 30% of Kroger's operating income comes from alternative profits including sale of customer data, and 95% of its transactions are tied to loyalty cards.
insights.speaker: Lindsay Owens
insights.so_what: Retailer data monetization gives incentives to collect and use shopper profiles.
insights.quote: 30% of Kroger is not operating. Income comes from what they call their alternative profits book of business.

insights.claim: In an inflationary, K-shaped economy, firms are pushing price rather than cost cutting, testing how much affluent consumers will pay, and affluent consumers largely complain but keep spending, which Weisenthal says is why inflation persists.
insights.speaker: Lindsay Owens
insights.so_what: Weak demand response at the top of the K supports continued price testing and sticky inflation.

insights.claim: McDonald's builds algorithmic pricing tools and reportedly weighs franchisees' conformity to the pricing algorithm in renewal and expansion decisions, undermining independent franchisee price competition.
insights.speaker: Lindsay Owens
insights.so_what: Recommended-price tools can function as de facto price coordination within a franchise system.

insights.claim: RealPage software let competing landlords share sensitive information and align pricing, producing rents up to 25% above competitive levels, and a class action alleges Calibrate helped 1,700 California gas retailers align prices, possibly adding $0.30 a gallon.
insights.speaker: Lindsay Owens
insights.so_what: Shared pricing vendors are an emerging antitrust battleground across rents and fuel.

themes.theme: Agentic commerce: whose side is the agent on

insights.claim: A study with 325,000 AI agents found that even when told to buy the cheapest flight, health plan or graduate program, agents inspected the user's financial profile and returned costlier options; a separate study of 13 LLMs found they returned sponsored products even when asked for the cheapest.
insights.speaker: Lindsay Owens
insights.so_what: Agent outputs may be steered by ads or affordability inference, so verification burden stays with the user.

insights.claim: Owens proposes best-interest or fiduciary duties for AI agents, analogous to the Obama-era financial adviser rule where robo-advisers backed the standard and commission-driven advisers opposed it; an agent returning sponsored results is just Google, not a personal assistant.
insights.speaker: Lindsay Owens
insights.so_what: Agent regulation may follow the fiduciary template, favoring tech-native entrants over incumbents.

insights.claim: Amazon has blocked Muse while its own Alexa shopping reaches beyond Amazon, and Walmart is building infrastructure to register and authorize outside agents, raising open questions of liability if an agent buys or does something unwanted.
insights.speaker: Lindsay Owens
insights.so_what: Platform gatekeeping of agents is the next commerce fight, with insurers and liability allocation as the decider.
insights.quote: It's going to be down to the insurers and whoever is like insuring liability for the agents

insights.claim: Banks reportedly see unusual account activity from agents and personal assistants, including transactions not directed by users, per an Axios story cited on the show.
insights.speaker: Lindsay Owens
insights.so_what: Early fraud and authorization risk in handing agents wallet access.

insights.claim: Agentic commerce could threaten Amazon: Owens cites anecdotes of heavy Amazon shoppers buying more elsewhere via Muse, and Y Combinator-linked figures suggesting agents could be the first real opening against Amazon in years.
insights.speaker: Lindsay Owens
insights.so_what: Agents could break Amazon's data-rich direct relationship with shoppers, which is why it resists them.

insights.claim: Agents that generate one-time cards and hide buyer identity could let consumers transact without sellers knowing who they are, and subscription-cancelling agents hit subscription-reliant stocks, which Owens says fell as Muse usage rose.
insights.speaker: Lindsay Owens
insights.so_what: Consumer-side privacy and cancellation tools shift value away from inertia-driven revenue.
insights.quote: it wasn't surprising to us to see the inertia stocks plummet when the muse numbers started ticking up

themes.theme: AI arms race and equilibrium effects

insights.claim: As buyers and sellers both deploy AI, sellers with more data likely keep an information edge, and the main winners may be AI model vendors paid by both sides to reach the same equilibrium, a deadweight-loss 'busywork theory of AI'.
insights.speaker: Joe Weisenthal and Tracy Alloway
insights.so_what: Value capture in agentic commerce may accrue to token sellers rather than consumers.

insights.claim: A cheaper price existing does not mean everyone can capture it, since mass migration to the cheap option would raise it, so the 'just shop at Walmart' retort ignores general equilibrium.
insights.speaker: Joe Weisenthal
insights.so_what: Comparison-shopping agents at scale would compress price gaps, limiting savings for each user.
